The Priceof Arrival

A data story for one person: someone deciding whether coming to Sydney is still worth it.

Who is actually arriving, and what does that mean for Mei?

Team DataLensKatherine LinJiajun XuYucheng LiuUTS · Data-Driven Storytelling
S1

Open on the headline everyone has seen: international student numbers at a record high. Our story is not for a policy analyst. It is for someone like us eighteen months ago, reading that headline and trying to decide whether coming here was still worth it.

Click: the board flips. The question we chase all the way through is who is actually arriving, and what that means for one person's decision.

Headlines answer a policy question. Mei has a personal one, and a mistimed application now costs a A$1,600 visa fee and possibly a year she can't get back.

Meet Mei, our primary persona, built directly from Journal 2's reader definition. Twenty-three, considering a Master's in Sydney, undecided.

Click through her four questions. Each is an insight from the empathy map (E1 to E4) and each becomes one act of the story, in the order she would actually ask them: headline, then where, then when, then cost.

Why worth analysing: public numbers are built for policy readers. With the visa fee rising from A$710 to A$1,600 and the Genuine Student test, the cost of a poorly timed decision is now substantial.

Mei, 23Master's in Sydney?

Pains

  • Torn between moving too early and missing her visa window
  • Trusts official data intellectually, but anecdote sways her emotionally
  • Wants one dollar figure, only ever gets an index

Gains

  • Can tell headline noise apart from her real visa deadline
  • Weighs the official number against forum stories instead of picking one
  • Knows what the index can and can't tell her, and stops waiting for a number that won't come

Built from real artifacts: headlines, forum threads, agent messages, policy milestones (visa fee, Genuine Student test, Ministerial Direction 111), plus our own experience applying to Sydney.

Walk quadrant by quadrant. The point to land: we wrote about her fear and her trust in sources, not about our charts. The most useful insight is a contradiction: she trusts official data with her head but anecdotes with her gut.

Every note carries an E-code, so it can be traced into a user story and a storyboard panel.

Index to a shared baselineJan–May 2019 = 100, so series of very different sizes can be compared.
Log-scaled spacelog10 choropleth and region × field heatmap, so small hubs stay visible.
Policy-annotated timelineEach dip in the grant rate sits under the decision that caused it.

Qualitative inputs for the empathy maps: media headlines, forum threads, agent communications, policy milestones, and our own experience applying to study in Sydney.

Five public datasets. Two from the Department of Education give us scale and geography; Home Affairs gives visa grant rates; ABS gives CPI and SA4 boundaries.

Three methods carry the analysis: indexing everything to January–May 2019 so different scales compare fairly; log scales so small hubs are visible next to the CBD; and putting policy dates directly on the visa timeline so cause sits next to effect.

Every dip has a date

US-M3 ✓Mei can point at a specific dip and name the policy beside it, instead of calling the trend "up" or "down".

Scene 5: Mei hears the rules are tightening and wonders whether it's just a bad time.

A line chart alone shows what changed, not why. Stacking the policy timeline under it lets the viewer connect each dip to the decision that caused it. Click through the three stamps: the Genuine Student test in March 2024, the fee jump to A$1,600 in July, and enrolment caps under MD111 in December.

It also keeps the chart self-contained: nobody has to take our word for the explanation.

Higher Education carries the "record student numbers" headline, yet only 22.3% of it is new. That is how total enrolments stay high while intake shrinks. Replaces Journal 1's Sankey, which implied a flow between two unrelated snapshots.

Scene 6: Mei and her agent look at sectors. Click: Higher Education, 177,204 enrolments, 61% of the NSW total, but only 22.3% are new commencements.

Click: at the other end ELICOS, 49.9% new. The sector that carries the headline is the one least dependent on new arrivals, which explains Act 1.

Method note: we replaced Journal 1's Sankey, which implied a flow between two unrelated annual snapshots, with paired stacked bars.

Act 4 · Rising insight E3 Figure 6 · Annual mean indices, 2019 = 100
S7
BeforeShe wants one dollar figure for a year of study and living.
Shift"How much of a financial buffer do I need for these changes?"

Prices rose faster than the crowd

Index, 2019 = 100 · 2026 = Jan–May meansABS CPI · Dept of Education
US-M4 ✓Mei can say costs rose faster than the student population, without mistaking the CPI index for a dollar cost. We withdrew a "monthly budget" promise in Journal 2 because this data cannot support it.

Scene 7: Mei wants an exact monthly number. Click: enrolments, falling to 78.4 in 2022 and recovering to 116.7 in 2025.

Click: Sydney All Groups CPI climbed steadily from 100.2 to 123.0 in 2025, and 126.7 in the first months of 2026. Click: rents from 99.8 to 114.9, then 117.6.

Honest limit: CPI is an index, not dollars. Mixed frequencies and baselines mean no causation. So the reframe is not "what will it cost" but "how big a buffer do I need".

The headline is only the starting point

Can visa timing, location, intake and affordability work together well enough to make the plan realistic?

The Aha moment. Bring back each lens with a click: the headline, location, visa timing, affordability.

The realisation: the challenge is no longer just whether Mei can get a place. It's whether visa timing, location, intake and affordability can work together well enough for the plan to be realistic. They can't be judged separately.

Four moves, each backed by a figure

Mei stops relying on headlines and brings the evidence to her family. The data now shapes a real decision.

WhenTime the application

Read your own intake against the policy timeline, with MD111 caps and the Genuine Student test in view.

Fig 4
WherePick a hub, not a city

Shortlist one or two SA4s where your field is actually taught, then search housing around them.

Fig 2–3
How muchBudget a buffer

Costs outran the student population. Plan for rising prices, not a single fixed figure.

Fig 6
Now or laterThis intake or wait?

Check how much of your sector is new intake before reading the headline as competition.

Fig 1 · Fig 5

Scene 9, recommendations for Mei. Four actions, each tied to a figure: reconsider timing using the visa and intake data; narrow campus and housing to the hubs in Figures 2 and 3; set aside a larger buffer based on cost trends; and use the sector data to answer "this intake or wait?"

04 · Recommendations For Daniel and the organisations around Mei

Charts that travel without us

US-S2 · Caption standard

Already applied to Figures 1–6 and kept for any figure added later.

COUNTS
NSW international student enrolments and commencements, head count
PERIOD
January–May each year, indexed to Jan–May 2019 = 100
EXCLUDES
Visa outcomes and where students live
SOURCE
Dept of Education monthly summary, 2026

US-S1 · One-slide export

Figure 5's lifecycle view, sized for a client deck, so agents explain headline vs real intake without building their own chart.

Wider value

  • Newsrooms: report commencements beside enrolments, so "record high" says who it counts
  • Universities & service planners: 85.8% of study happens in three SA4s; city-wide totals hide that
  • Agents: advise by sector and intake, with a policy timeline clients can read for themselves

For Daniel, two SHOULD stories. The caption standard: every caption says what is counted, the period, what is excluded and the source, because his charts travel without our text. And a one-slide export of the lifecycle view.

Wider value: newsrooms, universities and planners, and agents can each act on these figures.

04 · Recommendations What the data can't say, and what we'd do next

The limits we kept visible

01
An index is not a dollar figureCPI shows relative change. We withdrew a monthly-budget promise rather than overstate it.
02
Place of study, not residenceSA4 data shows where students study, not where they live.
03
2026 is partialJan–May means are not directly equivalent to a full year.
04
Patterns, not causationMixed observation frequencies and baselines limit comparisons.
ValidateTest both personas through interviews with international students and education agents.
SequenceStoryboard the panels before finalising empathy notes, so each note earns its panel.
InteractAn interactive version of the storyboard, like this one, so readers can step through Mei's journey.

Credibility comes from saying what the data can't do. Four limits we deliberately kept visible.

Click for next steps, drawn from our individual reflections: validate personas with interviews (Yucheng), storyboard earlier (Katherine), and make the storyboard interactive (Jiajun), which is what you're looking at.
